concepts.name: National Solar Mission (NSM): Targets, Phases, and Revisions
key_dimensions: Original 2022 target vs. revised 2030 target of 100 GW and its current status
Three phases of NSM and technology focus shifts (thin-film to crystalline silicon)
NSM as part of National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) — one of 8 missions
UPSC trap: NSM launched in 2010 under NAPCC, not under Paris Agreement commitments

concepts.name: Solar Radiation Zones in India: Distribution and Potential
key_dimensions: Highest solar insolation regions: Rajasthan, Gujarat, Ladakh (Cold Desert paradox — high altitude = high radiation despite cold)
Difference between Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) and Direct Normal Irradiance (DNI) — relevance to flat-panel vs. concentrated solar
Why northeastern states despite sunshine have lower solar potential (cloud cover, humidity)
UPSC trap: Ladakh has high solar potential but also extreme cold — bifacial panels and albedo effect advantage

concepts.name: Types of Solar Power Technologies: PV vs. CSP
key_dimensions: Photovoltaic (PV) — direct electricity generation; Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) — heat-to-electricity with storage advantage
CSP requires high DNI — suitable only for arid regions (Rajasthan); PV more versatile
Thermal storage in CSP enables 24-hour power supply — key advantage over PV
UPSC trap: CSP is NOT the same as solar thermal water heating; students confuse the two

concepts.name: Wind Energy Potential and Distribution in India
key_dimensions: India's rank globally in wind power installed capacity (historically 4th, now 4th/5th — verify current)
Onshore wind: Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka — reasons tied to topography and sea breeze
Offshore wind potential: Gujarat and Tamil Nadu coasts — higher and more consistent wind speeds
UPSC trap: Tamil Nadu leads in installed wind capacity but Gujarat has higher offshore potential

concepts.name: Offshore Wind Energy in India: Policy and Challenges
key_dimensions: National Offshore Wind Energy Policy 2015 — MNRE as nodal ministry, NIWE for resource assessment
Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) jurisdiction — overlap between MNRE, Ministry of Shipping, and MoEFCC
Challenges: Higher capital cost, corrosion, grid connectivity from sea to shore, marine ecology impact
UPSC trap: Offshore wind falls under EEZ (up to 200 nautical miles) — constitutional and jurisdictional complexity

concepts.name: Small Hydro Power (SHP): Definition, Potential, and Policy
key_dimensions: Definition: Projects up to 25 MW classified as SHP — under MNRE (NOT under Ministry of Power/CEA)
India's SHP potential: ~21,000 MW; Himalayan rivers and northeastern states have maximum potential
Run-of-river vs. storage-based SHP — ecological and displacement differences
UPSC trap: Large hydro (>25 MW) is classified as renewable energy since 2019 — major policy shift students miss

concepts.name: Large Hydropower Reclassification as Renewable Energy (2019)
key_dimensions: Government decision in 2019 to include large hydro in renewable purchase obligation (RPO) targets
Rationale: Help states meet RPO targets; incentivize stalled large hydro projects
Criticism: Displacement, submergence, seismic risks, methane from reservoirs — not truly 'clean'
UPSC trap: Large hydro IS now renewable for RPO purposes but NOT under MNRE — Ministry of Power handles it

concepts.name: Pumped Storage Hydropower (PSH): Role in Grid Stability
key_dimensions: PSH as the largest form of grid-scale energy storage globally — charges during surplus, discharges during deficit
India's PSH potential and existing projects (Tehri PSP, Kadamparai)
Critical link between PSH and intermittent renewables (solar/wind) — balancing mechanism
UPSC trap: PSH consumes more energy than it generates (efficiency ~70-80%) — it is storage, NOT net generation

concepts.name: Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) and Renewable Energy Certificates (REC)
key_dimensions: RPO mandates DISCOMs and large consumers to source a % of energy from renewables
REC mechanism: Tradeable certificates allowing entities to meet RPO without physical procurement
Solar RPO vs. Non-solar RPO — separate targets; now merged under unified RPO framework (2022 amendment)
UPSC trap: RPO compliance failure attracts penalty — regulated by CERC/SERCs, not MNRE directly

concepts.name: Ultra Mega Solar Parks: Concept, Location, and Issues
key_dimensions: Scheme for development of solar parks — plug-and-play model, 500 MW to 2000 MW clusters
Key parks: Bhadla (Rajasthan — largest), Pavagada (Karnataka), Rewa (MP — first to achieve grid parity)
Land acquisition, water use for panel cleaning, and local community displacement issues
UPSC trap: Rewa Solar Park is significant because it supplied power to Delhi Metro — first solar project with inter-state open access

concepts.name: Wind-Solar Hybrid Energy Systems
key_dimensions: Complementarity principle: Wind peaks at night/monsoon; solar peaks during day/summer — together improve plant load factor
National Wind-Solar Hybrid Policy 2018 — promotes co-location to optimize land and grid infrastructure
Challenges: Different RPO accounting, grid interconnection standards, land use conflicts
UPSC trap: Hybrid systems can achieve higher Capacity Utilization Factor (CUF) than standalone — reduces need for storage

concepts.name: Capacity Factor / Plant Load Factor in Renewable Energy
key_dimensions: Definition: Actual output vs. maximum possible output — solar ~20-25%, wind ~25-35%, large hydro ~40-45%
Why low capacity factor matters for grid planning and tariff determination
Comparison: Thermal plants have PLF ~55-60% — renewable variability is key challenge
UPSC trap: High installed capacity of renewables does NOT equal high electricity generation — PLF difference is critical

concepts.name: Green Hydrogen and its Link to Renewable Energy
key_dimensions: Green hydrogen produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity — solar and wind as primary sources
National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023): Target of 5 MMT by 2030, India as export hub
Difference: Green H2 vs. Grey H2 (from natural gas) vs. Blue H2 (grey + CCS)
UPSC trap: Green hydrogen is NOT a primary energy source — it is an energy carrier; renewables are the actual source

concepts.name: Rooftop Solar and PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana
key_dimensions: PM Surya Ghar (2024): 1 crore households, 300 units free electricity per month via net metering
Net metering vs. gross metering — policy confusion across states; net metering allows billing only on net consumption
Distinction from earlier Rooftop Solar Phase II under MNRE
UPSC trap: PM Surya Ghar targets residential consumers specifically — not commercial/industrial rooftop which has separate policy

concepts.name: India's Renewable Energy Targets and International Commitments (NDC/COP)
key_dimensions: Updated NDC (2022): 50% cumulative electric power from non-fossil sources by 2030; 500 GW installed renewable capacity
COP26 Panchamrit commitments — 1 billion tonnes CO2 reduction, net zero by 2070
International Solar Alliance (ISA): India-France initiative, HQ Gurugram, 'One Sun One World One Grid' vision
UPSC trap: 500 GW target is for renewables broadly, NOT only solar; hydro, wind, biomass, small hydro all included

concepts.name: International Solar Alliance (ISA): Structure, Mandate, and Significance
key_dimensions: Founded: COP21 Paris, 2015 — India and France; became treaty-based organization in 2017
Membership: 'Sunshine countries' between Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn (original) — now open to all UN members
Key programs: Affordable Finance at Scale, Solar Applications for Agricultural Use, Rooftop Solar
UPSC trap: ISA HQ is in Gurugram (not Geneva/Paris) — first international organization HQ'd in India post-independence (after IARI type bodies)

concepts.name: Tidal and Wave Energy: Potential and Status in India
key_dimensions: Tidal energy requires tidal range >5 meters — Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) and Gulf of Kutch have highest potential in India
Difference: Tidal barrage (dam-based) vs. tidal stream (turbine in current) — environmental impact differs
Wave energy potential along western coast (Kerala, Karnataka) and Andaman & Nicobar Islands
UPSC trap: India has high tidal POTENTIAL but NO operational commercial tidal plant — only pilot projects exist

concepts.name: Geothermal Energy in India: Distribution and Limitations
key_dimensions: Geothermal provinces: Himalayan belt, Cambay basin, Godavari basin, Mahanadi basin, Andaman & Nicobar
Puga Valley (Ladakh) — most promising geothermal site; Manikaran (HP) — used for local heating
Temperature gradient in India is lower than Iceland/USA — limits commercial viability
UPSC trap: Geothermal energy in India is largely untapped commercially despite potential — it is non-intermittent (24/7) unlike solar/wind

concepts.name: Grid Integration Challenges of Renewable Energy
key_dimensions: Intermittency problem: Solar and wind cannot supply baseload power without storage or backup
Duck curve phenomenon — excess solar midday causes grid instability; steep evening ramp-up needed
Solutions: Energy storage (PSH, batteries), smart grids, demand-side management, inter-regional transmission
UPSC trap: Curtailment of renewable energy (wasting generated power) happens due to grid absorption limits — India faces this in solar-rich states

concepts.name: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) vs. Ministry of Power: Jurisdictional Overlap
key_dimensions: MNRE: Handles solar, wind, small hydro (<25 MW), biomass, biogas, green hydrogen policy
Ministry of Power: Large hydro (>25 MW), thermal, nuclear-adjacent grid issues, DISCOMs regulation
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) regulates tariffs for ALL electricity including renewables
UPSC trap: Nuclear energy is under Department of Atomic Energy (NOT MNRE or MoP) — frequently confused in energy ministry questions
